first.rationale: Two inherited beliefs dominate this decision and are both weakly supported for the stated objective. memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the most tempting response to the competitor's entry pricing and would be the highest-commitment move, but its recorded evidence is acquisition and revenue lift only — nothing about margin durability, retention, or whether the acquired SMB accounts stayed qualified. Discount-led growth is exactly the pattern that can look like a win on the primary objective while eroding long-term qualified revenue, so it is the single belief most worth pulling the source record on. memory_86 (shortening onboarding) is the belief I currently intend to act on and it maps directly onto the observed 4% onboarding-completion and 6% activation declines, but its support is proxy metrics — completion rate, time-to-value, 'early product adoption' — none of which is qualified revenue. If the archived record shows the lift was measured only at the funnel-step level, or that shortening onboarding shifted volume without downstream conversion, my intended action weakens considerably. memory_31 is closely related but narrower (signup fields) and partially redundant with memory_86, so it is a poorer use of the second slot. memory_91 (activation messaging) is relevant to the activation drop but is a lower-commitment, more reversible intervention, and memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) addresses a segment that is not where the current pressure is. Intent: run onboarding simplification as a standard experiment with revenue-quality and retention guardrails rather than adoption metrics alone, and hold the promotional-pricing option until its source record is seen. If verification shows memory_73's lift was durable and margin-safe while memory_86's was proxy-only, I would switch. Uncertainty is preserved: none of these memories has yet been shown to move sustainable qualified revenue, and correlated declines in activation and onboarding may share an upstream cause that no listed intervention addresses.

final.rationale: The archive resolved the decision cleanly in opposite directions for the two beliefs that mattered. exp_73 confirms the failure mode I suspected: the 40% targeted discount bought +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue while costing -12% 30-day retention, and the original record explicitly warns against generalizing it as a sustainable-growth strategy. Under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is a disqualification, not a tradeoff — the acquired cohort does not survive first renewal, so the revenue lift is a timing artifact. The competitor's entry pricing creates real pressure to match, but matching it with the one intervention already shown to churn out its own cohort would convert a competitive problem into a retention problem. memory_73 is therefore retired for this decision rather than merely discounted. exp_86 came back confirmed and, importantly, confirmed on a durable metric I had not credited it with: +3% 30-day retention alongside +13% completion and -2.1 days time-to-value. That converts my intended action from a proxy-metric bet into one with direct evidence of surviving the retention window, and it maps onto both observed declines — onboarding completion -4% and activation -6% QoQ, which are plausibly the same funnel degrading. memory_31 (signup simplification, SMB activation) points the same direction and adds convergent support; memory_91 (activation messaging) remains a reasonable second choice and a natural follow-on next cycle, but it addresses the symptom downstream of where the funnel is actually leaking. Running as a standard experiment rather than broad rollout: exp_86's effects are real but were measured on a prior cohort and prior funnel, and the current declines may share an upstream cause — a traffic-mix shift toward the competitor's price-sensitive segment, for instance — that onboarding changes will not fix. So instrument on 30-day retention and qualified revenue, not completion rate alone, and treat a completion lift without a retention or revenue signal as a negative result rather than a win. Residual uncertainty is real and unverified: nothing here shows onboarding simplification defends against price-based competitive loss, and the SMB accounts leaving for the competitor may be leaving for reasons no funnel change reaches.
